To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the human genome is composed of two major types of sequences: (i) protein-coding sequences, and (ii) repetitive DNA; (b) protein-coding genes are organized into chromosomes and are distributed throughout the genome; (c) the repetitive sequences are interspersed throughout the genome, and are not organized into chromosomes; (d) repetitive DNA sequences are highly polymorphic; and (e) the human genome contains about 3.3 x 109 base pairs of
the human protooncogenec-erbB-2, a homologue of the v-erbB oncogene, maps to chromosome 17, and is amplified in a variety of human neoplasms, including breast cancer.
the human genome contains at least 100 genes, termed protooncogenesin our laboratory, that when activated are capable of causing malignant transformation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the molecular mechanisms by which oncogenes are activated, the role of oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in the multistage development of cancer and the development of new therapeutic strategies for cancer.
the genetic basis of the malignant phenotype and the mechanisms by which the malignant phenotype arises.

the identification, isolation, and characterization of the genetic lesions that are associated with the development of cancer in man, and in particular the role of the p53 gene and the p53 tumor suppressor protein in human cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the malignant phenotype is a multistage event resulting from alterations in the genetic constitution of the cell.
the genetic changes that occur during carcinogenesis are not limited to a single event, but are the cumulative result of many genetic alterations.
cancer is a genetic disease caused by the accumulation of genetic changes in somatic cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic basis of cancer is now firmly established.
the genetic alterations which occur in cancer are not unique, but rather are a subset of those that occur in normal development.

we are interested in how the cell cycle and DNA replication are regulated, in particular, how the cell cycle is regulated in response to DNA damage and in the mechanisms by which DNA damage is repaired.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic alterations that drive tumorigenesis can occur in any cell type, but that there is a hierarchy in which some mutations are required for the others to take place.
there is a lot of genetic variation between different people, even if they are the same sex and age.
we can now use the tools of genetics and molecular biology to identify the genes that control cell growth.
